title: Choosing Your Own Lottery Ticket
text:
In the early 1970s the psychologist Ellen Langer ran a series of studies on what she called the illusion of control: the tendency to act as if we can influence outcomes that are purely a matter of chance.

In one of her best-known studies, office workers at two companies in the United States were offered tickets for a lottery costing one dollar. The tickets were cards showing pictures of football players. Some participants chose their own card from a box; others were simply handed one by the experimenter. On the morning of the drawing, the experimenter went back to each participant and asked how much they would sell their ticket for, explaining that someone else wanted to buy in.

Every ticket had exactly the same chance of winning. Yet people who had picked their own card asked, on average, for more than four times as much money to give it up as people who had been handed a card.

In other studies in the same paper, Langer found that elements of skill, such as choice, familiarity, competition and active involvement, all increased people's confidence in winning games that were entirely random. People who drew cards against a nervous, awkward opponent bet more than those facing a confident one, although the game was pure chance. Langer argued that because skill and chance situations are often mixed in daily life, people carry the habits of skill into situations where they do not apply.
lesson: Making a choice, practicing or feeling involved can make random outcomes feel controllable. Before investing more, ask whether your actions actually change the odds or only your confidence.
source: Langer, E. J. (1975). The illusion of control. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 32(2), 311-328.
